core: The elements of design as the visual raw materials a designer works with, distinct from the design principles
Point: a precise location, visually a dot, the smallest building block and a potential focal point
Line: a mark connecting two points or tracing a movement; actual versus implied; direction and quality
Shape: an enclosed two-dimensional area with a boundary; geometric versus organic
Form: the three-dimensional element with depth and volume; implied form on a flat surface
Space: positive versus negative (white) space, and the figure/ground relationship
Value: lightness and darkness on a white-to-black scale; high-key versus low-key; value as the basis of implied form
Color treated as a single element (hue), with color theory left to the sibling topic
Size/scale mentioned as a relative element that becomes meaningful through comparison
supporting: The elements-versus-principles distinction (elements are the nouns, principles are how you use them)
That a full-color design can be reduced to grayscale and still hold together on value alone
That negative space is active, not empty, and is deliberately composed in logos and symbols
outOfScope: The principles of design such as balance, contrast, emphasis, hierarchy, rhythm, proximity, and Gestalt grouping (owned by graphic-design-and-digital-media:foundations:principles-of-design)
Color theory: the color wheel, harmonies, schemes, and color psychology (owned by graphic-design-and-digital-media:foundations:color-theory)
Typography and type as a design element (owned by graphic-design-and-digital-media:foundations:typography-basics)
Composition and layout strategy such as grids and the rule of thirds (owned by graphic-design-and-digital-media:foundations:composition)
Technical color management, RGB/CMYK gamut mapping, resolution, and file formats

claims.claim: The visual elements of design are the basic things that can be seen on a surface, and point, line, and plane (shape) are building blocks from which designers create images, icons, textures, patterns, diagrams, and typographic systems.

A point is a precise position or location on a surface; visually a dot, it is the basic building block of every variation of line, texture, and plane, and a focal point is the first place the eye is drawn to in a composition.

A line is a collection of points arranged linearly that connects two points or traces the path of a movement; it can be actual or implied, long straight lines are rare in nature and dominate when present, and thickening a line turns it into a plane (shape).
A shape (plane) is a flat, two-dimensional enclosed area with defined borders that can be geometric (circle, square, pyramid) or organic (a leaf), and a line that closes becomes a shape.
Form is the element related to shape but three-dimensional: it encloses volume and exhibits height, width, and depth, whereas a shape is two-dimensional; on a flat surface, form is implied.

Positive space is the space of the defined shape or figure, and negative (white) space is the area around and between shapes; the figure is always perceived in relation to its surroundings, so composing the negative space controls visual emphasis and energy (the figure/ground relationship).

Texture is both a visual and a tactile quality: actual (tactile) texture is a real surface quality felt by touch, including the choice of printed substrate, while visual (implied) texture is an illusion of surface created through line, shading, and color on a flat plane.

Value is the use of light and dark, running on a scale from white to black; lighter values are called high-keyed and darker ones low-keyed, and value gives a shape the illusion of mass and a composition its sense of light and shadow, independent of hue.

Color is a fundamental element referring to the use of hue; digital media uses the additive RGB system and print uses the subtractive CMYK system, and the two color spaces overlap but are not identical.

The elements of design (the visual materials) are distinct from the principles of design (the strategies for arranging them); the same textbook treats visual elements and compositional/organizational principles as separate sections.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact number and names of 'the elements' vary by source (point and size are sometimes included, sometimes omitted; the graphic-design textbook uses 'plane' where the art text uses 'shape').
positions: Graphic Design and Print Production Fundamentals emphasizes point, line, and plane and treats color, space (negative space), and texture as further visual elements, folding value into color/texture discussion.
The LibreTexts art text lists the classic seven visual elements: line, shape, form, space, texture, value, and color.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the widely taught canonical set (point/dot, line, shape, form, space, texture, value, color, with size noted as optional), drawing the definition of each from whichever source states it most clearly, and notes that 'plane' and 'shape' name the same two-dimensional element.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('Elements Of Design is a foundational concept... a simple way to apply it') with no substantive claims about any actual design element; all of it was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate placeholder definitions with sourced definitions of each specific element.
Added the elements-versus-principles distinction, which the draft omitted entirely.
Kept color to a single-element treatment and explicitly deferred color theory, typography, composition, and the design principles to their sibling topics to avoid duplication.
rightsIssues: Both sources are openly licensed OER (CC BY 4.0 and CC BY-SA 4.0), so facts may be reused with attribution; nonetheless all lesson wording is original and no source prose was reproduced.

No copyrighted images, logos, font files, or proprietary color values are reproduced. The FedEx figure/ground example that appears in the source textbook is not reproduced; the worked example uses an originally described generic poster instead.

sourceRecords.title: Graphic Design and Print Production Fundamentals, Section 3.2 'Visual Elements: Basic Things That Can Be Seen' (Alex Hass)
sourceRecords.provider: Graphic Communications Open Textbook Collective / BCcampus Open Education
sourceRecords.notes: Primary OER for this subject. Section 3.2 by Alex Hass defines point (a precise location, visually a dot, and the focal point concept), line (a collection of points that connects two points or traces a movement, actual or implied, thickening into a plane), plane/shape (a flat surface with defined borders, geometric or organic), colour (RGB additive vs CMYK subtractive systems that overlap but differ), negative/white space (the figure/ground relationship, with stable, reversible, and ambiguous types), and texture (a visual and tactile quality, including printed-substrate choice). The canonical opentextbc.ca host returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher; the section was read in full via the Internet Archive full-text copy (archive.org/stream/GraphicDesignAndPrintProductionFundamentals) on 2026-08-19. CC BY 4.0 confirmed from the book's About page. Facts synthesized; no prose reproduced.

CC BY-SA 4.0 confirmed from the page footer, read 2026-08-19. Used to source value and form as distinct elements and to cross-check the shape/space/texture definitions.
